blocks.text: A database MCP server sits in front of a real SQL database and lets an AI agent read data safely, without ever letting the model touch raw credentials.
It exposes tables and schemas as resources the agent can browse, and a single guarded tool for running actual queries.
This lesson opens the real world use cases in this module by showing exactly how that guarding works, and why it matters so much here.
1. What a Database MCP Server Is

blocks.alt: What a Database MCP Server Is
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441589331-114594168.png
A database MCP server is a thin translation layer between an AI agent and a SQL database such as Postgres, MySQL, or SQL Server.
It does not replace the database, it wraps it, deciding exactly what an agent is allowed to see and do against it.

items: Expose table and column structure so the agent knows what data exists.
Expose a controlled way to actually query that data.
Enforce limits the raw database driver would never enforce on its own.

blocks.text: Everything in this lesson follows from that one framing, the server is a gatekeeper, not just a pipe.
2. The Underlying System: A Real Database
Assume the underlying system is a production Postgres instance backing a normal business application, orders, customers, invoices, and so on.
That database already has its own users, permissions, and connection limits, the MCP server has to respect all of them, not work around them.
A good design treats the database as a system with its own operational rules, and builds the server as a careful guest, not the owner.
3. Tables as Resources
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441589331-946820171.png
Tables map naturally onto MCP resources, they are data an agent should be able to browse before it ever writes a query.
A resource for the orders table might return its column names, types, and a short description of what the table is for.

items: db colon slash slash tables slash orders, returns column names and types for the orders table.
db colon slash slash tables slash customers, returns the customers table schema.
db colon slash slash schema, returns the full list of tables available to this server.

blocks.text: Letting the agent read schema as a resource means it can write a sensible query on its first try, instead of guessing column names.
4. Safe Query Execution as a Tool
Actually running a query is an action with real side effects on database load, so it belongs behind a tool, not a resource.
The tool most database MCP servers converge on is called run_query, it takes a statement and returns rows.
Everything interesting about this lesson lives in how that one tool is built, because a careless run_query is a direct path to disaster.
5. Why Read Only Access Matters So Much Here

blocks.alt: Why Read Only Access Matters So Much Here
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441589331-719186227.png
An agent that can only read data can still cause real harm, a runaway query can lock rows or exhaust connections, but it cannot destroy data.
An agent connected with write access, even briefly, can delete rows, corrupt tables, or drop a table entirely from one badly formed instruction.

blocks.title: Read only is a design decision, not an afterthought
blocks.content: The database connection the run_query tool uses should be created with a role that physically cannot write, so a bug in the tool logic can never turn into a write.

blocks.text: This is the same principle from the Access Control lesson earlier in this module, the safest permission is the one that was never granted in the first place.
6. Why Query Validation Matters
A read only role stops writes, but it does not stop an agent from writing a query that scans an entire multi million row table.
Query validation is the second layer of defense, it checks the shape of the query itself before anything touches the database.

blocks.text: This layered approach mirrors the Resource Security lesson, never rely on a single control when a second cheap one is available.
7. Designing the run_query Tool Schema
A good schema for run_query keeps the query text and its values completely separate, which is the whole point of parameterized queries.
Notice params is its own field, the model is never asked to build a full query string with values already baked in.
8. Parameterized Queries to Avoid Injection
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441589332-537878247.png
SQL injection happens when untrusted text is concatenated directly into a query string, letting an attacker or a confused model smuggle in extra SQL.
Parameterized queries avoid this entirely, the database driver binds values separately from the query text, so a value can never change the query structure.

code.content:
import psycopg2

READ_ONLY_DSN = "postgresql://mcp_reader:secret@db-replica.internal:5432/appdb"

def run_query(query, params, row_limit=500):
    normalized = query.strip().lower()
    if not normalized.startswith("select"):
        raise ToolError("only select statements are allowed")
    if query.rstrip(";").count(";") > 0:
        raise ToolError("multiple statements are not allowed")

    conn = psycopg2.connect(READ_ONLY_DSN)
    try:
        with conn.cursor() as cur:
            cur.execute("SET statement_timeout = 5000")
            cur.execute(query, params)
            rows = cur.fetchmany(row_limit)
            columns = [desc[0] for desc in cur.description]
            return {"columns": columns, "rows": rows}
    finally:
        conn.close()

blocks.text: The call cur dot execute of query comma params passes params as a separate argument, the driver handles safe binding, the model never touches raw SQL escaping.
A matching call from the agent might look like run_query with a select on orders where region equals a placeholder, and params holding just the region value.
9. Enforcing a Read Only Database Role

blocks.alt: Enforcing a Read Only Database Role
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441589926-418989939.png
The parameterization above only stops injection, the role below is what actually makes writes impossible at the database level.

items: mcp_reader is never granted insert, update, delete, or drop on anything.
The default privileges line covers tables created later, so new tables stay read only automatically.
This role should be its own database user, never the same credential the application itself writes with.

blocks.text: 10. Query Timeouts and Row Limits
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441589928-957075607.png
A read only, validated query can still be a bad query, a select with no filter across a huge table can still lock resources for seconds.
Two simple guardrails handle this, a statement timeout on the connection, and a hard row limit on what the tool returns.

items: Set statement_timeout on every connection the tool uses, five seconds is a reasonable default.
Cap row_limit server side, even if the agent asks for more, never trust a client supplied limit blindly.
Return a clear message when a query is cut off by the limit, so the agent knows to narrow its filters.

blocks.text: 11. Schema Introspection as a Resource
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441589929-746957795.png
The schema resource itself should be generated from the database, not hand maintained, so it never drifts out of date.

code.content:
SELECT column_name, data_type
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_name = 'orders'
ORDER BY ordinal_position;

blocks.text: Running this against information_schema and caching the result for a few minutes gives every resource read fresh, accurate structure.
12. Handling Errors from the Database
A database can fail in several distinct ways, and a good tool response tells the agent which kind of failure it is dealing with.

items: Validation error, the query was not a select or used a forbidden pattern, tell the agent exactly what to fix.
Timeout error, the query ran too long, suggest adding a filter or narrowing the date range.
Connection error, the database itself is unreachable, tell the agent to retry later rather than rewrite the query.
Empty result, zero rows matched, this is a success, not an error, and should be returned as such.

blocks.text: Conflating these into one generic error message is the single fastest way to make an agent retry the same broken query forever.
13. Real World Use Case: Answering Business Questions
The clearest use case for this server is a business user asking a plain question and an agent turning it into a safe query on live data.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Business question","What the agent does"],"rows":[["How many orders shipped last week","Reads the orders schema resource, then runs a filtered count query"],["Which customers spent the most this quarter","Runs a grouped, ordered select with a date range parameter"],["Is any invoice overdue right now","Runs a select filtered on due date and payment status"]]}

blocks.text: In every row, the agent reads structure first, then calls run_query once with parameters, never by hand assembling SQL text.
14. Auditing and Logging Every Query
Every call to run_query should be logged with who asked, what query ran, and how many rows came back.
This log is often the only way to answer a question later like which agent session pulled this data and when.
15. Common Extensions and Where to Draw the Line
Some teams eventually want a narrow write path, approving a refund, updating a status field, through its own separate, tightly scoped tool.
That write tool should never share a connection or a schema with run_query, keep the read only surface and the write surface completely separate.

items: Add a second, purpose built tool for any specific write action, never widen run_query itself.
Keep the read only role and any write role on entirely different database credentials.

blocks.text: Worked Example: An Agent Answering a Revenue Question
A support lead asks the agent what total revenue looked like for the west region last month.
The agent first reads the orders table resource to confirm the column names for region, amount, and created_at.

code.content:
run_query(
  query="select sum(amount) as total from orders where region = %s and created_at >= %s and created_at < %s",
  params=["west", "2026-06-01", "2026-07-01"],
  row_limit=10
)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","What happens"],"rows":[["Schema read","Agent confirms column names before writing the query"],["Validation","Server confirms this is a single select statement"],["Execution","Query runs against mcp_reader with a five second timeout"],["Response","One summed row returned, agent phrases the answer in plain language"]]}

blocks.text: No SQL text ever contains a raw region name or date, both travel as bound parameters the whole way through.
Common Mistakes
These mistakes show up constantly the first time a team wraps a database in MCP.

items: Connecting run_query with the same credential the application uses to write, instead of a dedicated read only role.
Letting the agent build query strings with values already inserted, instead of passing params separately.
Skipping a statement timeout, so one bad query can hold a connection open indefinitely.
Returning a single generic error for every failure, which hides whether the agent should retry or rewrite.
Allowing multiple statements separated by semicolons in one query string.
Hand maintaining the schema resource instead of generating it from information_schema.

blocks.text: Practice
Design a run_query tool for a database that also stores employee salary data, and decide what changes.

items: Stretch goal one, should the read only role expose every table, or should some tables be excluded entirely from the schema resource.
Stretch goal two, sketch how you would add a strict row limit that cannot be overridden by a value the agent passes in.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway
A database MCP server is safe because of layered, boring controls, a read only role, parameterized queries, validation, timeouts, and logging, working together.
None of these controls are exotic on their own, the skill is remembering to stack all of them rather than trusting just one.
